sermon:
## The Indictment Read Aloud
*When God puts His own people on trial*

**Text:** Isaiah 1:1-20 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 5:1-7 · Amos 5:21-24 · Micah 6:6-8 · Psalm 51:16-17

The book opens not with comfort but with a courtroom. Heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses, and the One who has been wronged is the One who made everything. This is not a prophet venting at his culture. This is a Father with a charge to bring against children He raised. And the first sound out of His mouth is not thunder. It is grief.

**The wound is a Father's wound**
Listen to how it begins. "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth; for the LORD has spoken: 'Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know, my people do not understand.'" (Isaiah 1:2-3) Read it slowly and you feel the sting of it. The animal in the stall knows where its food comes from. The covenant people do not. God does not say first that they broke a rule. He says they do not know Him, and the donkey does better. This is a Father who taught a child to walk, and the child cannot find his way home. The prophets across the centuries all heard this same wound. Micah heard it as a lawsuit pleaded before the mountains: "O my people, what have I done to you? How have I wearied you? Answer me." (Micah 6:3) The indictment is real, but it is grieved before it is angry. A passage about God's anger that itself reads only as rage has missed the heart of it. The Father is not winning an argument. He is mourning a household. And the household He is mourning over is not pagan Babylon. It is the very people who carry His name, who keep His feasts, who know the words of His law by heart. That is what makes the grief unbearable. A stranger who never knew you cannot betray you. Only a child can.

**Worship as noise**
Here is the part that should arrest anyone who has ever led a service or filled a pew. They were not irreligious. The temple was busy. The offerings were many. The calendar was full of feasts. And God says: stop. "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the LORD; I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams and the fat of well-fed beasts... Bring no more vain offerings; incense is an abomination to me. New moon and Sabbath and the calling of convocations, I cannot endure iniquity and solemn assembly." (Isaiah 1:11-13) The smoke that was meant to please Him He calls an abomination. The festivals He commanded He now says His soul hates. Why? The next lines tell you. "When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you; even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood." (Isaiah 1:15) They had perfected the machinery of devotion while their justice rotted underneath it. Amos heard the same verdict in his own generation: "I hate, I despise your feasts, and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies... But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream." (Amos 5:21-24) God is not against worship. He is against worship offered by hands that crush the poor on the way to the altar. And we have learned to do this. We can sing on Sunday with money taken unjustly on Friday and feel devout the whole time. The song does not cancel the theft. The smoke does not cover the blood. The fifth chapter says it as a song that turns to a verdict, God planted a vineyard, dug it, cleared its stones, built a watchtower, cut a winepress, did everything a vinedresser could do, and then "he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry." (Isaiah 5:7) He looked for fruit and got rot. He looked for justice and got the cry of the crushed. That is the church on a bad century. That is me on a bad week, leading the singing while the outcry goes up from somewhere I would rather not look.

**Come, let us reason, the mercy inside the indictment**
And then, mid-trial, the strangest turn in the chapter. The Judge who has every right to convict does not slam the gavel. He opens His hand. "Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool." (Isaiah 1:18) This is the room I live in. I have stood behind a pulpit and called things by softer names than they deserved, because the hard name cost more. I have made justice optional and worship loud. I have had hands full of one kind of blood or another and spread them out in prayer as though God could not see them. The wonder of this chapter is not that He indicts us, He has every right. The wonder is that the indictment ends with an offer to be made clean: scarlet to snow, crimson to wool, and the offer is real. But it does not come cheap, and Isaiah will not let us think it does. "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword." (Isaiah 1:19-20) The cleansing is offered, not assumed. This is where the whole book is already pointing. The hands full of blood will be washed, but not by harder scrubbing, and not by louder feasts. There is One coming whose own blood does what our sacrifices never could. The temple could give God the smoke. It could never give Him the one thing He wanted: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise." (Psalm 51:17) The cross would.

Religion cannot cover blood-stained hands.

## Undone in the Doorway
*What happens to a man who actually sees God*

**Text:** Isaiah 6:1-13 · **Supporting:** Exodus 33:18-20 · Revelation 4:8 · Luke 5:8 · Romans 10:14-15

There is a kind of religion that wants God close and tame, near enough to comfort, never near enough to wound. Isaiah 6 is the cure for it. A man walks into the temple he has worshiped in his whole life, and for one moment the veil thins, and what he sees does not warm him. It wrecks him. And the wrecking is the mercy.

**The throne and the trembling**
The date is given, and it matters. "In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and the train of his robe filled the temple." (Isaiah 6:1) Uzziah had reigned for fifty-two years. He was the only king most people in Judah had ever known, and now he was dead, and the throne of the nation sat empty. Into that political vacuum Isaiah is shown the throne that is never empty. The earthly seat had gone vacant. The heavenly one had not. And around it the seraphim, the burning ones, covered their faces, because even sinless creatures cannot stare at this. "And one called to another and said: 'Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.'" (Isaiah 6:3) Hebrew has no superlative the way English does. To say a thing once is to state it. To say it twice is to stress it. To say it three times is to push the word as high as language can climb. God is not merely holy. He is holy, holy, holy, set apart beyond the reach of comparison. The foundations of the threshold shook at the voice. The house filled with smoke. John would be carried up to the same throne centuries later and hear the same threefold cry from the same creatures (Revelation 4:8). This is not a metaphor for a moving moment in a service. This is the floor of reality, and it is shaking.

**The cry of a ruined man**
Now watch what seeing it does to a good man. Isaiah was the most articulate person in Judah. Words were his calling, his gift, his trade. And the very first thing the vision takes from him is his mouth. "And I said: 'Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts.'" (Isaiah 6:5) Not woe to them, woe to me. He does not point at the corrupt court or the faithless nation, though both were real and he knew it better than anyone. He sees himself first. He pronounces over his own life the very word, woe, that the rest of the book will pronounce over the nations. This is the mark of every true encounter with holiness. The prophet Isaiah in the eighth century before Christ and the fisherman Peter on a lake centuries later say the same thing in the same posture: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord." (Luke 5:8) When Moses asked to see God's glory, God warned him, "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." (Exodus 33:20) Isaiah is finding out why. The nearness of holiness does not flatter the one it comes near. It exposes him. And I have stood in pulpits and described God's holiness as if I had survived it, as if I were reporting from a safe distance about a fire I had not actually walked into. I had not. The day it actually lands, you do not feel qualified. You feel undone. Anyone who walks away from a vision of God impressed with himself did not see God. He saw a mirror.

**The coal, and the cost of being sent**
Here is the gospel buried in the throne room. The undone man is not left undone. "Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. And he touched my mouth and said: 'Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for.'" (Isaiah 6:6-7) The very fire that should have consumed an unclean man is brought to him as cleansing. Grace does not lower the holiness to make Isaiah comfortable. It pays for the access. And notice where the coal comes from, the altar, the place of sacrifice, the place where blood was shed. Cleansing comes from the place of death. Only then, mouth cleansed by something he did not earn and could not earn, does he hear the question and answer it. "And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?' Then I said, 'Here I am! Send me.'" (Isaiah 6:8) But look hard at what he is sent into, because it is not what we want. Not revival. Hardening. "Go, and say to this people: 'Keep on hearing, but do not understand'... Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed." (Isaiah 6:9-10) The cleansed mouth is sent into a field that will not yield, to preach until the cities lie waste and the land is desolate. The coal does not buy him an easy ministry. It buys him a costly one. This is the shape of the cross, centuries early, a clean One sent to an unhearing people, bearing the altar's fire so the unclean could come near, and paying for it the whole way down. Paul knew the chain depended on the sent one: "How are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent?" (Romans 10:14-15) Isaiah is the first answer to that question, and the answer cost him. The call still does.

Holiness ruins before it sends.

## The Sign a Frightened King Refused
*Immanuel, God with us before we asked for Him*

**Text:** Isaiah 7:1-14 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 8:11-13 · Isaiah 9:2 · Isaiah 9:6-7 · Matthew 1:22-23

There is a kind of fear that disguises itself as faith. King Ahaz had it. Two enemy kings, Syria and Israel, were marching on Jerusalem to topple him, and his heart and the heart of his people "shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind." (Isaiah 7:2) Into that fear God sent a prophet with an offer almost too generous to believe, and Ahaz, dressed in piety, said no.

**The refusal that sounds religious**
God could not have made the offer more open-handed. He sends Isaiah to steady the trembling king with a word, "Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint" (Isaiah 7:4), and then He extends a blank check no other king in Scripture is given. "Ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven." (Isaiah 7:11) Name it, Ahaz. Reach as low as the grave or as high as the sky, and God will meet the request to prove He can be trusted with this crisis. And the king answers, "I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test." (Isaiah 7:12) It sounds humble. It even quotes the principle of not testing God. It is unbelief in a Bible verse. Ahaz had already made up his mind to trust Assyria's army instead of Judah's God, and he dressed his decision in piety so no one could argue with it. We do exactly this. We call our fear discernment. We call our refusal to obey prudence. We reach for the most spiritual-sounding sentence available to cover a decision we made out of terror. Isaiah saw straight through it, and the warning he gives in the next chapter is the cure for it: "Do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread. But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread." (Isaiah 8:12-13) The king was managing his fear with chariots and treaties. God was offering Himself, and the king said no thank you. And this is the quiet tragedy of the religious heart: it can hold a true doctrine in one hand and use it to push God away with the other. Ahaz did not lack theology. He lacked trust. He believed God existed and refused to believe God could be relied on, which is the most respectable form of unbelief there is, because it never has to call itself unbelief at all.

**The sign God gives anyway**
Here is the mercy that runs right over the top of human refusal. Ahaz would not ask, so God gives the sign unasked. "Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." (Isaiah 7:14) Immanuel, God with us. Stop on that name. Not God watching from a safe distance while we sort out the geopolitics. Not God sending help. God with us, in the siege, in the mess, in the dark, in the body. Ahaz wanted deliverance from his two enemies, the kind he could see arriving with an army. God promised something larger and slower and far harder to control: His own presence, arriving as a child. The deliverance Ahaz craved was a strong battalion. The deliverance God planned was a baby. And Matthew, reading this prophecy with the eyes of one who had seen it land, knew exactly who that child finally was. "All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel' (which means, God with us)." (Matthew 1:22-23) The sign offered to a faithless king in the eighth century before Christ was waiting all along for a manger in Bethlehem. There would be a closer fulfillment in Ahaz's own day, a child born in his lifetime whose growth marked the clock on his enemies' defeat. But the name was too large for that child to carry alone. Immanuel, God with us, is not the kind of name a nation gives to a boy who simply grows up to see two kings fall. It waited for the One it actually described.

**The government on infant shoulders**
Follow the light a little further into chapter nine, and the promise grows from a sign into a kingdom. "The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone." (Isaiah 9:2) Not a light they generated. A light that dawned on them while they sat in the dark, the way morning comes to people who did nothing to earn the sun. And the source of it is named with titles that buckle the mind: "For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace." (Isaiah 9:6) Read those titles slowly, because they are laid on the shoulders of an infant. Mighty God. Everlasting Father. The government of the universe resting on a child small enough to be carried. This is the scandal the whole passage has been building toward, and I have to put myself inside it instead of admiring it from across the room. I am Ahaz more often than I want to confess from a pulpit, offered the presence of God and choosing the manageable solution, the alliance I can see, the army I can count, the verse that excuses the cowardice. And God keeps answering my unbelief the way He answered the king's: with a gift I did not ask for and did not deserve. He came as a child, to people who would not have asked, into a darkness that could not put Him out. "Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end... The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this." (Isaiah 9:7) Not the zeal of a faithful king. The zeal of the Lord, who saves us in spite of our refusals.

God comes as a child.

## Life From a Stump
*What grows after the axe falls*

**Text:** Isaiah 11:1-10 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 10:33-34 · Isaiah 6:13 · Isaiah 12:2-3 · Romans 15:12

Isaiah ends chapter ten with the sound of a forest coming down. Assyria, the proud axe God had used to discipline His people and then judged for its arrogance, is itself felled. "Behold, the Lord GOD of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power; the great in height will be hewn down, and the lofty will be brought low. He will cut down the thickets of the forest with an axe, and Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One." (Isaiah 10:33-34) Everything tall is brought low. The towering empire comes down like timber. And then, in the quiet after the great trees fall, the very next word is not about a tree still standing. It is about a stump.

**The stump nobody expected**
"There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit." (Isaiah 11:1) Read the name carefully. It does not say the stump of David. It says Jesse, David's father, the man before the dynasty, the obscure shepherd from Bethlehem whose youngest son nobody bothered to call in from the field. The royal line that had grown into a great tree is pictured here as a hacked-off stump, cut down to the root, the kingdom apparently finished. And out of the dead-looking wood, life. A green shoot where there should be nothing but a scar. This is how God works, and we are slow to believe it because we keep looking at the part that still stands tall. Earlier in this same book Isaiah had been told the whole nation would be felled like an oak, burned down, reduced to almost nothing, "but the holy seed is its stump." (Isaiah 6:13) That is the pattern of God's mercy stated as a single image. Hope is never in the part of you that is impressive and standing. Hope is in what survives the axe, the buried seed in the cut-down stump. We resist this because we are taught to admire the tall tree and bet on the strong line. But God's whole way of working in this book runs the other direction. He brings down what is high and brings up what is low. He fells the proud forest of Assyria and then grows His King out of a stump nobody was watching. The cross is the same shape, centuries on: a life apparently ended, a hope apparently cut to the ground, and then a green shoot on the third day from wood everyone had written off.

**The King the Spirit rests on**
What grows from the stump is not merely survival. It is a Ruler unlike any Judah ever crowned. "And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD." (Isaiah 11:2) Every gift the kings of Israel had lacked, this one carries in full. And it changes how He governs. "He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear, but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth." (Isaiah 11:3-4) Every king before Him had been swayed by the rich man's robes and the powerful man's voice, ruling by appearances and rumor. This one cannot be bought, cannot be flattered, cannot be deceived, and He sides with the poor and the meek, not as a campaign slogan but as a settled verdict. "Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins." (Isaiah 11:5) Paul saw exactly who this stump-born King was, and that He was for the nations and not Israel only: "The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope." (Romans 15:12) The shoot from the stump is Christ, born, against every human odd, in Jesse's own forgotten town of Bethlehem.

**The kingdom where the wolf lies down**
Then the vision opens wider than any throne room, out into the whole created order. "The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the lion and the fattened calf together; and a little child shall lead them... The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra." (Isaiah 11:6-8) Predator and prey, the oldest enmity written into the world, undone. The child who should fear the snake plays at its den. "They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea." (Isaiah 11:9) This is not a slightly improved world. It is a healed creation, where the violence woven into nature itself is unwritten by the reign of the righteous King. And I have to ask honestly where I stand in that picture, because for most of my life I am the wolf in it, not the lamb, guarding my territory, baring my teeth, calling the aggression strength and the defensiveness wisdom. The kingdom that grows from the stump does not flatter the wolf. It tames him. And the only fitting response when a cut-down tree puts out a living branch and the wolf lies down beside the lamb is the song Isaiah places at the very end of this section: "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation. With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation." (Isaiah 12:2-3) We thought it was finished when the forest came down. The stump was alive the whole time.

New life grows from the stump.

## The God Who Weighs Empires
*Why no nation gets the last word*

**Text:** Isaiah 13:9-11 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 14:12-15 · Isaiah 19:1 · Isaiah 23:9 · Daniel 4:35

We like our God local. We like Him invested in our nation, attached to our side, present at our ceremonies, fond of our flag. Isaiah 13 through 23 is a long, patient dismantling of that idea. Oracle after oracle marches past, against Babylon, against Moab, against Damascus, against Egypt, against Tyre, and the cumulative weight of them lands as a single sentence the people of Judah needed to hear and we need to hear: the Holy One of Israel is not a tribal deity. He is the Sovereign of every empire that ever marched, and He weighs them all on the same scale.

**Babylon, the superpower, brought down**
The section opens against the greatest power of the coming age, an empire that thought itself permanent. "Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it... I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless." (Isaiah 13:9-11) Babylon called itself eternal. God calls it pomp. And then comes one of the most haunting passages in all the prophets, a taunt sung over a king who reached for the rank of God: "How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, you who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high... I will make myself like the Most High.' But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit." (Isaiah 14:12-15) Count the times he says "I will." The climb is all self-assertion, and it ends in the pit. This is the script every human empire eventually reads aloud. "I will ascend." And every single one of them is brought down to the ground. The taunt is sung over a Babylonian king, but it reaches back past him to the first reach for godhood and forward past him to the last. It is the oldest sentence in the human heart, spoken in Eden in a softer form, you will be like God, and it has been the engine of every tower and every throne since. The reach is always upward. The fall is always downward. The pit is always where it ends.

**Every power, no exceptions**
Watch how God moves through the nations and leaves not one of them standing on its own legs. Egypt, the ancient civilization men assumed would outlast time itself: "Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them." (Isaiah 19:1) The gods of the Nile shake when the true God merely arrives. Tyre, the merchant city that had turned commerce into a religion and wealth into a throne: "The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth." (Isaiah 23:9) Moab's pride, Assyria's boasting, Babylon's towers, God names each one and weighs each one. This is not score-settling, and it is not God playing favorites between rival countries. It is order. The God who made the nations weighs the nations, and the thing the scale measures every time is pride, the same pride that built Babel and said let us make a name for ourselves, the same pride that whispers "I will ascend." Generations later Daniel would watch this very God humble this very kind of king, and put the verdict into one sentence: "All the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing, and he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, 'What have you done?'" (Daniel 4:35)

**The mirror in the oracle**
It is dangerously easy to read these chapters as God taking sides against other people's countries, to cheer when He levels the empire I dislike and go quiet when His scale tips toward the one I salute. That is the trap, and it is the trap of every age. Remember who the first nation on trial in this book was: Judah, His own covenant people, indicted in chapter one. The pride God will not tolerate in Babylon is the same pride He will not tolerate in His own house, or in mine. I am quick to feel righteous when God brings down the empire across the sea and slow to feel His weight pressing on the one whose anthem I know by heart. But the Holy One does not check my passport before He weighs my pride. He measures me on the same scale that measured Babylon. And here, precisely here, the section turns toward grace, because the God who shatters every false climb to heaven is the very God who would one day come down Himself, not ascending to seize a throne, but descending to a manger and a cross to win one. The Servant of the chapters ahead does not say "I will ascend above the stars." He empties Himself and goes down. The kings of the earth reach up and fall into the pit. The King of heaven reaches down and lifts us out of it. Babylon's day star fell out of heaven by grasping. The true Morning Star came down out of heaven on purpose, to save the very people whose empires He weighs. This is the verdict the whole section has been building toward, and it is the verdict that should keep me humble before every flag I am tempted to baptize: the God who weighs Babylon and Egypt and Tyre is not the property of any nation, and the only One who ever climbed down instead of up was the One we hung on a cross for refusing to be the king we wanted.

Every empire answers to him.

## The Feast on the Mountain
*Two cities, and which one swallows death*

**Text:** Isaiah 25:6-9 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 24:1-3 · Isaiah 26:3-4 · Isaiah 27:1 · 1 Corinthians 15:54

There are two cities running through these chapters, and you live in one of them right now. There is the city of chaos, proud, fortified, certain of itself, built by human hands to keep disorder out, and there is the city of God. Isaiah 24 lays the first one in ruins. Isaiah 25 spreads a table in the second. Everything in your life depends on which city you have quietly built your security inside.

**The city of confusion, broken open**
Chapter 24 is not gentle, and it is not meant to be. It is the whole earth coming apart at the seams. "Behold, the LORD will empty the earth and make it desolate, and he will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants." (Isaiah 24:1) And then a line that cuts straight through every distinction we hide behind to feel safe: "And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the slave, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller... as with the lender, so with the borrower." (Isaiah 24:2) The judgment does not check your title or your tax bracket. Priest and people, master and slave, the one who lends and the one who owes, all of them flattened by the same wave, because none of those roles is the foundation any of us thought it was. "The wasted city is broken down; every house is shut up so that none can enter... The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart, the earth is violently shaken." (Isaiah 24:10, 19) This is the city of chaos, the proud, ancient human project of building security without God, and the verdict is that it cannot stand. We are still pouring our lives into it. Every system we trust to keep death and disorder at bay, every fortress of wealth or status or control, is this city, and Isaiah says its foundation is sand.

**The feast where death is buried**
Now watch the camera lift from the rubble to the other mountain, and everything in the air changes. "On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined." (Isaiah 25:6) Notice it is not a feast for Israel only, for all peoples, the very nations God was weighing and judging chapters earlier, now drawn to a table. And at this feast the host does the one thing no human power has ever managed in all of history. "And he will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations. He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth." (Isaiah 25:7-8) Read that again. Death, the thing that swallows everything and everyone, the appetite that has never been satisfied, is itself swallowed up. The grave does not get the last meal. God does. And then the God of the universe bends down and wipes the tears off faces, one by one, the way a parent leans over a child's bed in the dark. Paul could not hold himself together when he saw the day this prophecy finally came true at an empty tomb: "Then shall come to pass the saying that is written: 'Death is swallowed up in victory.'" (1 Corinthians 15:54) That is Isaiah's word, quoted by an apostle standing on the far side of a resurrection. The prophet saw the feast from a distance and named it as promise. Paul saw the firstfruits of it in an empty grave and named it as fact. Same mountain, same God, same swallowing of death, only now with a date in history and a stone rolled away.

**Which peace, and where it holds**
So the question these chapters press into your chest is simple and unavoidable. Which city are you trusting? The proud one looks unbreakable right up until the day it breaks, and then every house is shut up and no one can enter. The other looks, from a distance, like a feast you are not sure you are allowed to attend. And the difference between living in fear and living in peace is laid out in one of the most quoted lines Isaiah ever wrote: "You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock." (Isaiah 26:3-4) An everlasting rock, set against a city of sand. I have built in the city of chaos more than I want to admit in front of a congregation, leaning my security on things that empty out and houses that get shut up, calling it responsibility. The mercy of this passage is that the feast is spread for all peoples, which means it is spread for the man who has wasted years building in the wrong city. God will deal with the ancient enemy at last, "In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea." (Isaiah 27:1) And the One who finally slays the dragon and swallows death does it not by avoiding the grave but by going down into it Himself. The host of the feast paid for our seat at the table with His own life. "It will be said on that day, 'Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us. This is the LORD; we have waited for him; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation.'" (Isaiah 25:9)

Death itself is swallowed up.

## The Cornerstone and the Refuge of Lies
*Where Judah ran when it was afraid*

**Text:** Isaiah 30:1-3 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 28:16-17 · Isaiah 31:1 · Isaiah 30:15 · 1 Peter 2:6

When a nation is frightened, it does not usually become more faithful. It becomes more practical. Judah, with Assyria bearing down on it, did the sensible, reasonable, defensible thing. It went shopping for an army. It sent its envoys south to Egypt, to the horses and chariots that could be counted and inspected and depended on, and it called this strategy. And God, through Isaiah, names that strategy for exactly what it is, rebellion wearing the clothes of prudence.

**The alliance God calls sin**
Hear how He frames it, because the framing is the whole sermon. "Ah, stubborn children, declares the LORD, who carry out a plan, but not mine, and who make an alliance, but not of my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin; who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt." (Isaiah 30:1-2) Notice carefully what the charge is and is not. The charge is not that the plan is poorly thought out. It is that it is not His plan, made not of His Spirit, and that they never once asked Him. They added sin to sin by being competent without being faithful. Chapter 31 names the idol underneath it: "Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD." (Isaiah 31:1) The horses were real. The chariots were genuinely many and strong. That was precisely the problem. They could see the help waiting in Egypt, and they could not see God, so they trusted what their eyes could count. "Therefore shall the protection of Pharaoh turn to your shame, and the shelter in the shadow of Egypt to your humiliation." (Isaiah 30:3) There is a bitter irony folded into that word Egypt. Egypt is the house of slavery, the place God once brought them out of with a mighty hand. And now, in their fear, they are running back to the very house God redeemed them from, asking the old slavemaster for shelter. Fear does this. It makes us go back to the thing we were rescued from and call it safety.

**The rest they refused**
And here is the line that ought to break your heart, because it shows you what they turned down. "For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, 'In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.'" (Isaiah 30:15) That was the offer on the table. Returning. Rest. Quietness. Trust. The strength of a people who could finally stop running because their God was real and present and able. And the verse does not end where we wish it ended. "But you were unwilling." Three words that indict me as deeply as they indicted Judah. God held out rest with both hands, and the people chose the frantic, exhausting safety of chariots they could touch. "And you said, 'No! We will flee upon horses'... and, 'We will ride upon swift steeds'; therefore your pursuers shall be swift." (Isaiah 30:16) I have done this in seasons of fear, built my refuge out of the things I could control, defended it, maintained it, called it wisdom and stewardship, while the rest God was offering sat untouched in the corner because trust felt like weakness and waiting felt like doing nothing. Every refuge of lies feels like prudence on the way in. It only reveals itself as a lie when the storm finally hits and the shelter washes out from under you: "And I will make justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line; and hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter." (Isaiah 28:17) The hail does not negotiate with how reasonable the shelter seemed.

**The stone that holds**
But God does not leave Judah, or us, with only the demolition of our false shelters. In the middle of these very woes, between the swept-away refuges, He lays down something the hail cannot touch. "Therefore thus says the Lord GOD, 'Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion, a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: Whoever believes will not be in haste.'" (Isaiah 28:16) A tested stone, proven, weight-bearing, already passed through the trial. A sure foundation, against a city of sand. And mark the description of the one who builds on it, because it is the exact opposite of the Egypt-runners: he "will not be in haste," will not panic, will not bolt for the visible help, will not flee upon horses. The man trusting the cornerstone can stand still in the storm, because his security is no longer something he has to keep building. It is already laid, already tested, already bearing weight, and his only task is to believe it and not bolt. Peter, writing to frightened scattered Christians centuries later, tells us whose cornerstone this finally is: "For it stands in Scripture: 'Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.'" (1 Peter 2:6) The stone is Christ. So the choice set before Judah is the same choice set before me every time fear knocks: the chariots I can count, or the cornerstone I have to trust. One is fast and visible and impressive, and it washes out in the flood. The other is tested, and it holds when everything I built with my own anxious hands is swept downriver. And the returning and rest God offered Judah is the same rest the Son would later hold out in His own voice, come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. The cornerstone learned to speak.

Egypt's horses cannot save you.

## A Highway Through the Wilderness
*The road God builds where there was none*

**Text:** Isaiah 35:1-10 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 34:8 · Isaiah 35:3-4 · Matthew 11:4-6 · Hebrews 12:12-13

Chapter 34 is a desert made entirely of judgment. Edom, the old enemy nation, is turned back into wilderness, its streams to pitch, its soil to burning sulfur, its land to smoke that goes up forever, "for the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion." (Isaiah 34:8) It is bleak, scorched, hopeless ground. And then, with no transition but the turning of a single page, chapter 35 plants a garden in that wasteland. The violence of the contrast is the whole point. The same God who can dry up a green and prosperous land can flood a dead one with life.

**The desert that breaks into bloom**
Listen to the dead ground come alive. "The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus; it shall blossom abundantly and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the majesty of Carmel and Sharon." (Isaiah 35:1-2) This is not a desert that gets a little merciful rain and turns slightly less brown. This is a desert that sings, that takes on the glory of the greenest places in the land. And the word spoken to the people standing in the dryness is the steady refrain of this whole book to the afraid: "Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to those who have an anxious heart, 'Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come with vengeance, with the recompense of God. He will come and save you.'" (Isaiah 35:3-4) The trembling are not commanded to manufacture courage out of nothing. They are told the reason to be strong, because God Himself is coming, and He is coming to save the very people too weak to save themselves. This is the difference between the cheap encouragement of the world and the comfort of God. The world says be strong because you have it in you. Isaiah says be strong because Someone is coming who does. The order matters. Courage that rests on my own dwindling reserves runs out exactly when I need it most. Courage that rests on the God who is on His way holds when everything in me has already given out.

**The bodies that are healed**
Then the prophecy gets specific, and physical, in a way that should make any reader who knows the Gospels sit straight up in the chair. "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy. For waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert." (Isaiah 35:5-6) Blind eyes opened. Deaf ears unstopped. Lame legs leaping like a deer. Silent tongues breaking into song. The whole catalog of human brokenness, undone. Centuries after Isaiah wrote it, a man sat in a prison cell, his faith wavering, and sent messengers to ask Jesus whether He was really the one they had waited for. And Jesus did not answer with an argument. He answered with this chapter walking around in flesh: "Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me." (Matthew 11:4-6) He simply pointed at Isaiah 35 happening in front of him. The desert was blossoming. The bodies were leaping. The promise had a pulse and a face. And He added one line Isaiah did not write, blessed is the one who is not offended by me, because the way this Servant fulfilled the promise was not the way John expected, and it would not be the way we expect either. The desert blooms, but not on our schedule. The healing comes, but it comes through a man who would be despised before He was crowned.

**The highway home, and who it is for**
And through the blooming desert God lays a road, because deliverance is not only healing, it is being brought home. "And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it. It shall belong to those who walk on the way; even if they are fools, they shall not go astray." (Isaiah 35:8) Here is the tenderness hidden in the engineering: the road is built so plainly, so straight and clear, that no one stumbles off it, "even if they are fools, they shall not go astray." This is not a highway for the impressive and the capable. It is a highway for the ransomed, and the writer of Hebrews reached back and picked up its very image to strengthen tired, faltering believers: "Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed." (Hebrews 12:12-13) I know the wilderness in these verses from the inside, because I have made deserts out of green places with my own anxious unbelief, dried up my own gardens with worry and fear. The hope this chapter holds out is not that I will be clever enough to find my own way out of the waste. It is that God builds the road in, lays it straight enough for a fool to walk, and carries the ransomed all the way home. "And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away." (Isaiah 35:10) The Servant who would open the blind eyes is the same one who became the Way itself, the road home for people who could never find it alone.

God turns wilderness into highway.

## The Letter Spread Before the Lord
*One king, two seasons, two hearts*

**Text:** Isaiah 37:14-20 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 36:18-20 · Isaiah 38:1-5 · Isaiah 39:5-7 · 2 Corinthians 12:9

Hezekiah is one of the better kings in the whole story of Judah, and that is exactly what makes his account so dangerous to read comfortably. He shows us that faith in the crisis is no guarantee of faith in the calm. The same man can trust God completely when the enemy army is camped at his gate and then forget Him utterly the moment the danger lifts and the visitors bring gifts.

**The blasphemy at the wall**
The crisis comes first, and it comes loud and personal. The Assyrian field commander stands at the wall of Jerusalem and mocks not only the city's defenses but its God to His face. "Beware lest Hezekiah mislead you by saying, 'The LORD will deliver us.' Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?... Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?" (Isaiah 36:18-20) Hear what he is doing. He is filing the living God of Israel among the dead idols of all the nations Assyria has already crushed. Your God, he sneers, is just one more local god, and I have beaten every one of them so far. It is the oldest taunt in the world, and it lands on a king who knows full well he has no army that can stand against Assyria in the open field. What makes the moment so dangerous is that the taunt is half true. Assyria really had crushed god after god, nation after nation, and every shrine in its path had proven empty. By every visible measure the field commander's logic was sound. The only flaw in it was the one thing he could not see, that the God of Jerusalem was not one of the gods he had already beaten.

**The letter on the temple floor**
Now watch precisely what Hezekiah does, because this is the high-water mark of his entire life. A threatening letter arrives from the Assyrian king, and the king of Judah does not first convene a council of war or send a frantic appeal back to Egypt. "Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD." (Isaiah 37:14) He spreads the threat open in front of God, physically lays the enemy's words out on the temple floor, the way a man would lay an impossible, ruinous bill in front of the one person alive who could actually pay it. And then he prays the prayer of a man who knows exactly where he stands in the universe: "O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made heaven and earth... So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD." (Isaiah 37:16, 20) Look at the motive in that last line. Not merely save us so we survive, save us so they will know who You are. He wants the Assyrian taunt answered not for his own comfort but for God's name. And God answered. The angel of the LORD went out, and the great army that had blasphemed Him was simply gone by morning. Crisis faith, and God honored it to the hilt.

**The treasures and the pride**
If the story ended right there, it would do nothing but encourage us, and we would all want to be Hezekiah. But it does not end there, and the second half is the warning. The siege lifts. Hezekiah falls deathly ill and pleads with God, weeping, and God mercifully adds fifteen years to his life (Isaiah 38:1-5). And then, in the calm and the comfort and the relief, envoys arrive from rising Babylon with a get-well gift, and the king who once spread the enemy's threatening letter before the Lord now spreads his own glory before the future enemy. "And Hezekiah welcomed them gladly. And he showed them his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his whole armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them." (Isaiah 39:2) Everything. Nothing held back, nothing hidden, nothing referred to God. And Isaiah arrives with the sentence: "Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD. And some of your own sons... shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon." (Isaiah 39:6-7) The very man who trusted God in the storm sowed the seeds of the exile in the sunshine. And I know this man far too well, because I am this man. I have prayed like a saint with the impossible bill spread out on the table, and then strutted like a fool the moment it was paid, showing off the storehouse God filled as though I had filled it myself. The hardest season in which to trust God is not the crisis. It is the comfort. The strength Paul learned in his own weakness runs in exactly the opposite direction from Hezekiah's slide: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." (2 Corinthians 12:9) Hezekiah was strong in his weakness at the wall and weak in his strength in the palace. So am I, more often than I will say out loud.

Faith in crisis, pride in peace.

## Comfort for a People Going Into the Dark
*The God who does not grow tired*

**Text:** Isaiah 40:1-11 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 40:6-8 · Isaiah 40:28-31 · Mark 1:2-3 · 1 Peter 1:24-25

The whole book turns on its hinge here. The first thirty-nine chapters have been, in large measure, indictment and warning and judgment, a people loaded with iniquity walking step by step toward an exile they earned. And then chapter forty opens its mouth, and the tone breaks like a fever in the night. The very God who pronounced the sentence is the first one to speak tenderness over the condemned.

**Comfort, and a voice in the wilderness**
"Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins." (Isaiah 40:1-2) The word translated "speak tenderly" is, in the Hebrew, to speak to the heart, the same phrase used for a man wooing the woman he loves, speaking past her defenses to the frightened center of her. That is how God addresses a people headed into the dark. And then a voice cries out across the wilderness: "A voice cries: 'In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God.'" (Isaiah 40:3) Mark opens his entire Gospel by reaching back and seizing this exact verse, because the voice crying in the wilderness turned out to be John the Baptist, clearing the road for the One who was finally coming (Mark 1:2-3). The comfort God promised was never merely a better mood. It was a person on His way to us.

**The grass withers; the Word stands**
But comfort that lies to you is not comfort at all, and Isaiah refuses to lie to a frightened people about what they are. He tells them the truth about their own frailty first, and only then offers the hope. "A voice says, 'Cry!' And I said, 'What shall I cry?' All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever." (Isaiah 40:6-8) You are grass. Your strength, your beauty, your achievements, your nation, grass, and the wind is already coming across the field. That is not cruelty. It is the only solid ground real hope can stand on, because it pries your trust off the thing that withers and fixes it to the only thing that does not. Peter quoted these exact words to scattered, suffering Christians in his own day to steady them (1 Peter 1:24-25). The comfort holds precisely because everything else does not. When you finally stop trusting the grass, the Word that stands forever can hold your full weight. We spend most of our strength trying to keep the grass from withering, propping up our health, our reputations, our nations, our youth, as though enough effort could exempt one blade from the wind. It cannot. And the day we stop pretending it can is the day the real comfort can finally reach us, because it has nothing to do with the grass at all.

**The God who carries, and never tires**
And then the chapter rises to its full height with a question that exposes how small we have quietly let God become in our imaginations. "Have you not known? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable." (Isaiah 40:28) Here is the beating heart of the chapter for an exhausted, exiled, used-up people, and for every one of us who has come to the end of ourselves: your God does not run out. You do. He does not. The strength He gives is not a strength you generate and then spend. "He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength. Even youths shall faint and be weary, and young men shall fall exhausted; but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint." (Isaiah 40:29-31) The young and the strong, who have the most stamina of anyone, still fall down exhausted. The ones who wait on the Lord do not, because their strength is not their own. I come to this chapter empty more often than I would like to confess from a pulpit, depleted, faithless, half-convinced the warfare will never actually end and the exile will never lift. And it does not answer me by telling me to try harder or dig deeper. It tells me to wait, and it points me to a Shepherd. "He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young." (Isaiah 40:11) The everlasting God who never grows weary stoops all the way down and carries the lambs Himself, against His chest, gently. That Shepherd has a name, and He would say it of His own self one day standing on a hillside in Galilee, looking out over people who were harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd. I am the good shepherd, He would say, and the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. The everlasting God who does not grow weary would grow weary in a body, sleep in a boat, weep at a grave, and carry the lambs all the way to a cross. The comfort of chapter forty is not that God stays untouched above our exhaustion. It is that He came down into it, took it on, and still did not let go.

Our God does not grow weary.

## The Servant Who Will Not Break the Bruised Reed
*The living God against the dead idols*

**Text:** Isaiah 42:1-4 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 41:21-24 · Isaiah 44:14-17 · Isaiah 46:3-4 · Matthew 12:18-21

These chapters stage a courtroom, and the question on trial is the most important one a frightened exile could ask: which gods are actually real? The LORD summons the nations and their idols into court and sets one test that no false god in history has ever passed. Tell me the future. Declare what is coming before it comes. "Set forth your case, says the LORD; bring your proofs, says the King of Jacob. Let them bring them, and tell us what is to happen. Tell us the former things, what they are... or declare to us the things to come. Tell us what is to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods." (Isaiah 41:21-23) And the idols stand there in silence, because they cannot. "Behold, you are nothing, and your work is less than nothing; an abomination is he who chooses you." (Isaiah 41:24)

**The idols that cannot save**
Isaiah is merciless, and almost darkly funny, about the idols, because he desperately wants the exiles to see how foolish their fear of these things really is. Picture it the way he draws it: a man goes out and cuts down a tree, and "part of it he takes and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it; he makes it an idol and falls down before it... And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it. He prays to it and says, 'Deliver me, for you are my god.'" (Isaiah 44:15-17) He burns one half of the log to roast his dinner and warm his hands, and then bows down and prays to the other half of the same log to save his soul. "All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit." (Isaiah 44:9) But the point Isaiah is driving toward is sharper than mere mockery. The idols are dead weight. They have to be cut, shaped, nailed down so they will not topple, and carried everywhere their owner goes. And here is the great reversal that runs through the whole section: the false gods must be carried by their worshipers, while the true God carries His.

**The God who carries from the womb**
Listen to the tenderness of how He makes the contrast, addressing exiles who are terrified Babylon's gods have won. "Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb: even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save." (Isaiah 46:3-4) That single passage holds the entire difference between an idol and the living God in one image. You carry your idol, you make it, prop it up, defend it, haul it from town to town. God carries you, from before you were born to the gray hairs at the end, the whole length of a human life, never setting you down. Every false thing I have ever trusted, I had to carry: prop it up, defend it, maintain it, drag it around behind me. God has been carrying me the entire time I imagined I was the one carrying my faith. This is the quiet exhaustion underneath so much religion, people hauling around a god they have to keep upright, defending him, explaining him, propping him against the wind, and calling the strain devotion. Isaiah says: that is an idol, no matter how true its name. The living God is the one who carries you, not the one you carry.

**The Servant who will not break us**
And right into the middle of this courtroom of nothing-gods, God introduces His answer to the dead idols, not another argument, but a Servant. "Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations." (Isaiah 42:1) And then the gentleness that has made hardened men go quiet for thousands of years: "He will not cry aloud or lift up his voice, or make it heard in the street; a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice." (Isaiah 42:2-3) Hold those two pictures. The idols cannot save a single soul; this Servant will not crush a single broken one. The bruised reed, the bent, half-snapped stalk that any other power would break off and throw away as useless, He steadies and lets stand. The faintly burning wick, the little smoking flame the world would pinch out and be done with, He cups His hand around and keeps alive. Matthew watched Jesus moving quietly among the broken, the sick, the ones nobody else wanted, and he saw this very prophecy walking the roads of Galilee: "He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory." (Matthew 12:19-20) I have been the bruised reed, bent and nearly snapped through. I have been the dim wick, down to the last curl of smoke and sure I was about to go out. And the verdict of these chapters falls on both my fear and my failure at once: the gods I am tempted to fear are nothing, the God I am tempted to forget is carrying me still, and His Servant comes not to finish off the broken but to be gentle with them all the way to victory.

Idols are nothing; God carries.

## The Man of Sorrows in Our Place
*Pierced for the transgression that was ours*

**Text:** Isaiah 53:4-6 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 49:6 · Isaiah 50:6 · Isaiah 53:10-11 · 1 Peter 2:24

We come now to the summit the whole book has been climbing toward from its first page. The Servant has been promised since chapter forty-two; the light to the nations announced in chapter forty-nine. Here, in the song that spans the end of chapter fifty-two and all of fifty-three, we finally see what it costs Him to save. And what we see is not a conquering king on a horse. It is a man crushed beyond recognition, and the crushing, every blow of it, is for us.

**The one we turned away from**
Isaiah tells us in advance that we will not want Him, that He will come in a form our instincts reject. "For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not." (Isaiah 53:2-3) We hid our faces. Not just the Romans who drove the nails, not just the crowd that shouted in the courtyard, we. Isaiah pulls the entire human race into the rejecting crowd and refuses to let any of us watch from the gallery as innocent bystanders. The Servant comes in a form so far from our idea of a savior that our deepest instinct is to look away from Him. He had already foretold exactly what He would endure when He came: "I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting." (Isaiah 50:6) He saw the whole humiliation coming, and He walked into it with His eyes open and His face set.

**The great exchange**
And here, in these verses, is the center of the entire Christian faith, written down seven centuries before a single nail was ever driven. "Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed." (Isaiah 53:4-5) Read every preposition slowly, because the gospel itself lives in the prepositions. Our transgressions, His piercing. Our iniquities, His crushing. The chastisement was His; the peace it bought is ours. The wounds were torn into His flesh; the healing flows into ours. This is not the tragedy of a good man caught in a corrupt system. It is a substitution, a great exchange, a deliberate trading of places. He stood in the dock where I was supposed to stand and took the verdict that had my name on it. And then comes the line that names precisely what every one of us is: "All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all." (Isaiah 53:6) Every one to his own way, that is the most exact, most economical definition of sin anywhere in the Bible, and it is not a doctrine. It is autobiography. I went my own way. You went yours. And the iniquity that should have crushed each of us, God gathered up and laid on Him.

**Crushed by the Father, vindicated by life**
We must not soften the next part, however much it unsettles us to read it plainly. The cross was not an accident the Father failed to prevent. "Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand." (Isaiah 53:10) The Father was not absent at Calvary, wringing His hands at a miscarriage of justice. The Father was the one who laid the iniquity there and willed the offering. The Servant did not die as a helpless victim of circumstance; He died as a deliberate offering for guilt, and it was the Lord's own will and the Lord's own love that drove it. But the song does not end in the grave, and this is the turn that changes everything: "Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities." (Isaiah 53:11) He bears the iniquity; we are accounted righteous. That is the whole transaction of salvation compressed into one verse, His record and ours swapped at the cross. And this Servant was never meant for Israel alone: "It is too light a thing that you should be my servant... I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth." (Isaiah 49:6) Peter, a man who actually watched it all happen with his own eyes, said it as plainly as it can be said: "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed." (1 Peter 2:24) I cannot stand outside this chapter and admire it the way one admires great poetry from a distance. I am the sheep that turned to its own way. The wounds described here are mine to be healed by, and the One who took them did it on purpose. Every other religion in the world tells you to climb, to earn, to clean yourself up enough to be received. This chapter tells you the climbing has already been done by Another, in the wrong direction, downward, into the place of guilt, on your behalf. The Servant did not ask the sheep to find their own way back. He went out into the wilderness where they had wandered and took the iniquity onto Himself. That is not a story we would have written. It is too costly to be our invention, and too merciful to be anything but God's.

By his wounds we are healed.

## Come, Buy Without Money
*The grace that costs everything you are*

**Text:** Isaiah 55:1-7 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:11 · Isaiah 58:6-7 · Isaiah 59:1-2 · Revelation 22:17

The Servant has finished His work in chapter fifty-three. He has borne the iniquity, made the offering, accounted the many righteous. And now, standing on the ground that He purchased with His own wounds, God throws open a door and begins calling out into the street. The invitation is for everyone with nothing, which turns out to be the only requirement, and somehow the hardest one any of us is willing to meet.

**The invitation to the empty-handed**
"Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price." (Isaiah 55:1) Read it twice, because on the surface it makes no economic sense, and the nonsense is precisely the point. Buy, without money. Eat and drink the richest things, wine, milk, water, and pay nothing. The currency of this kingdom is not what you bring to the counter; it is your thirst and your emptiness. The only people who cannot come are the ones who insist they already have enough. That is the strange exclusion at the heart of grace. The door is wide enough for every thief and every failure and every wasted life to walk through, and too narrow for the one self-satisfied soul who believes he has paid his own way and needs no water. Emptiness is the ticket. Self-sufficiency is the one disqualification. And God knows exactly where we go instead, where we spend ourselves dry: "Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food." (Isaiah 55:2) We pour out our whole lives buying things that never feed us, working ourselves to exhaustion for what cannot fill us, while the one thing that actually satisfies is standing open and free in the street. And the invitation has a clock on it, an urgency: "Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near." (Isaiah 55:6) The door is open, but it is not open forever and not open on our timetable. Grace is free, but it is not casual. There is a nearness of God that is offered now and may not be offered indefinitely, and the gentlest invitation in the Bible carries inside it a warning we are slow to hear: come now. The thirst you feel is not an interruption to your life. It is the kindest thing about it, the very ache that could carry you to the water.

**The fast God actually wants**
But grace this free is never grace that leaves you exactly as it found you, and Isaiah will not let anyone hear "without money" and conclude that God therefore asks nothing of a life. A few chapters on, in chapter fifty-eight, God confronts a people who fast diligently and pray fervently and then complain that heaven seems not to notice. The answer cuts: their religion floats untethered above their injustice. "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him, and not to hide yourself from your own flesh?" (Isaiah 58:6-7) Free grace does not produce idle, self-absorbed religion. It produces people whose hands fall open toward the hungry exactly the way God's hand fell open toward them. The man who has truly drunk the free water cannot then close his fist against the thirsty man beside him; the two go together, or neither is real. A fast that leaves the oppressed in their chains and the hungry at the gate is not devotion God refused to notice. It is devotion God refuses to accept. The water of chapter fifty-five costs no money at all. It costs your tight, white-knuckled grip on yourself.

**The wall that only sin builds**
And then chapter fifty-nine names the single thing that can keep a person standing outside this wide-open door, and it is never, ever God's reluctance to let them in. "Behold, the LORD's hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear dull, that it cannot hear; but your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear." (Isaiah 59:1-2) God is not far off, distracted, or too busy. The wall between us and Him exists, but we built it, and we built it out of ourselves. This is where the whole sweeping invitation suddenly turns personal and painful, because it means the only thing standing between me and the free water is me, my sin, my self-rule, my unwillingness to walk up to the counter empty-handed and admit I have nothing to pay with. God's arm is not too short to reach me. My pride is too long, and it holds Him off. The grace that costs no money costs the one thing I am most unwilling to surrender, which is the management of my own life, the running of my own story. And the Servant already settled the bill, "by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, for he shall bear their iniquities" (Isaiah 53:11), so the price was never the obstacle. The surrender is. The same open call still goes out at the very last page of the whole Bible, in nearly the same words Isaiah used: "The Spirit and the Bride say, 'Come.' And let the one who hears say, 'Come.' And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price." (Revelation 22:17) Come empty, or do not come at all.

Grace costs nothing but yourself.

## The Year of the Lord's Favor
*Light rising on a world that cannot make its own*

**Text:** Isaiah 61:1-4 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 60:1-3 · Isaiah 65:17-19 · Isaiah 66:22-23 · Luke 4:18-21

The book ends in a place exile cannot follow, not in a merely rebuilt city, but in a remade creation. After sixty chapters of indictment and comfort, of judgment and the wounds of the Servant, Isaiah lifts his eyes one final time to a light no human hand could ever kindle and a world no human power could ever build. The man who opened in a courtroom closes in a new heaven and a new earth.

**Arise, the light has come**
"Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you. For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise upon you, and his glory will be seen upon you." (Isaiah 60:1-2) Mark carefully where the light comes from. The darkness is real and total, it covers the whole earth and lies thick over all the peoples; this is not a minor gloom that a little human effort could brighten. The light does not rise up out of the darkness, as though humanity might generate its own dawn if it tried hard enough. It rises upon the darkness from outside, the way the sun comes up over a sleeping country that did nothing whatsoever to summon it. And then the nations, the very same nations God weighed and judged back in the middle of the book, come walking toward the light: "And nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising." (Isaiah 60:3) The empires that climbed and fell now move toward a brightness they could never have manufactured. This is the answer to every age that believes it can build its own dawn, that with enough progress, enough effort, enough light of its own making, it will finally outrun the dark. Isaiah says the dark is thicker than that, deep enough to cover the whole earth, and the only light that ever pierces it comes from outside the system entirely, risen upon us, not generated by us. We do not light the morning. We wake up inside it.

**The Anointed One reads His own commission**
And then the source of the light opens His mouth and speaks for Himself. "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of the LORD's favor." (Isaiah 61:1-2) We are not left to guess who is speaking, because one ordinary Sabbath in the synagogue of Nazareth, a carpenter's son stood up to read, was handed the scroll of Isaiah, unrolled it to exactly these words, read them aloud to His neighbors, rolled it back up, sat down, and said one sentence that split history in two: "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing." (Luke 4:21) The Anointed One of Isaiah 61 is Jesus of Nazareth, and He stood up in His hometown and claimed these words as His own job description. Good news to the poor. Liberty to the captives. Sight to the blind. The year of the Lord's favor, opened, in person, in Galilee, in flesh. And there is one detail in how He read it that should not be missed. The scroll says "the year of the LORD's favor, and the day of vengeance of our God," but in Nazareth He stopped reading mid-sentence, at favor, and rolled the scroll up before the day of vengeance. The day of judgment is coming, and Isaiah names it. But the year of favor came first, and it came open-handed, and the One who closed the scroll on vengeance to announce favor was the same One who would later absorb that vengeance into His own body so the favor could reach us. And what He gives in place of the old griefs is total: "to grant to those who mourn in Zion, to give them a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the garment of praise instead of a faint spirit." (Isaiah 61:3)

**A new heavens and a new earth**
And from there the book climbs to its final, breathtaking vision, the promise that nothing broken stays broken forever, that the whole groaning creation gets not a repair but a resurrection. "For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind. But be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create... I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress." (Isaiah 65:17-19) Not a patched-up world, not the old order cleaned and reused, but a new one, where the former troubles do not even rise into memory. The very tears God promised to wipe away back on the mountain in chapter twenty-five, He now wipes away for good and forever. "For as the new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me, says the LORD, so shall your offspring and your name remain." (Isaiah 66:22) I sit here at the end of this enormous book and I cannot pretend for a moment that I belong to the light by anything I have done. I am one of the people the thick darkness covers, and the only reason there is dawn breaking over me at all is that the light rose from outside, in a Servant who was pierced so that the prison door could be opened. The same hands that this book began by indicting back in chapter one are the hands that get carried, washed and forgiven, into the new creation at the end. We did not build it. We did not earn the year of favor. He makes it, He proclaims it, He completes it from first page to last, and the final word of the prophet who opened in a courtroom is a world where the weeping is over for good and the worship never stops, "from new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath." (Isaiah 66:23)

He makes all things new.
